segments.speaker: John
segments.text: In a graduate seminar on embodied perception and robot learning, today's lecture is on TouchScale: 500 Hours of Human Vision and Touch for Visual-Tactile Learning. Recent work such as MAPLE: Encoding Dexterous Robotic Manipulation Priors Learned From Egocentric Videos and EgoDex: Learning Dexterous Manipulation from Large-Scale Egocentric Video shows how the field is scaling up first-person human data. Researchers from institutions including Google DeepMind and Texas A&M University ask a complementary question: what if those recordings also captured touch? Yes, Noah?

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Hi Professor, if egocentric video is already scaling, what does touch add that cameras cannot reliably tell us?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: A camera records visible movement, but contact is often hidden: it may show a hand holding a cup without revealing exactly where pressure falls or how firmly the fingers grip. TouchScale pairs first-person video with measurements from sensors worn on both hands. Its collection contains about 500 hours, 87,000 episodes, and 1,964 task descriptions, giving researchers a shared resource to study how vision and touch work together.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The collection spans more than 1,500 objects, roughly 20 participants, and varied environments, from kitchens and workbenches to offices and bedrooms. Repeated activities change object positions, layouts, and grasp choices, so the data includes meaningful variation rather than one fixed demonstration. The central contribution is not just volume: the same wearable sensing and synchronization pipeline is used throughout, making it easier to examine the effect of adding data without mixing incompatible collection protocols.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Quick question: what exactly do the participants wear, and how are the streams synchronized?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The system records head-mounted video with depth, video from cameras on both wrists, and tactile measurements from flexible gloves. Each glove has 880 sensing points across the fingers and palm, with less than 2 millimeters of spatial resolution. Video runs at 30 frames per second; touch is recorded at 50 hertz wirelessly or 100 hertz by wire. The streams are synchronized, and the original timestamps are retained.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The authors test three broader ideas. First, can tactile patterns learned from one glove transfer to a different sensor? Second, can touch prediction improve visual features used for action recognition? Third, can human vision-and-touch recordings help a robot policy even without human action labels? In that final test, the human data trains a tactile prediction pathway, while robot demonstrations are still used afterward to train the policy for the target tasks.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: So the human recordings teach the robot about contact, but not which movements to make?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Exactly. The tactile-prediction experiment trains TouchAnything on TouchScale or EgoTouch, then evaluates the models on EgoTactile without further training. Since the sensors differ, their measurements are mapped into 12 shared anatomical hand regions for comparison. Against a size-matched EgoTouch model, TouchScale improves contact overlap from 0.134 to 0.181 and volumetric overlap from 0.185 to 0.243, while also reducing localization and pressure errors.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: How should we interpret the zero-shot result if the two datasets use different sensor layouts?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: That difference is part of the challenge the experiment addresses. Models keep each dataset's native tactile layout during training, then predictions are compared using the shared hand regions. This makes the evaluation less dependent on matching sensor grids, though it cannot remove every difference between collection setups. Increasing TouchScale training data also raises zero-shot contact overlap on EgoTactile from 0.311 at 10% of the data to 0.383 at the full scale.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The second experiment asks whether tactile supervision transfers beyond touch prediction. Hiera B visual encoders are pretrained on TouchScale and three comparison datasets with the same prediction objective, initialization, and training budget. On three action-recognition benchmarks, TouchScale pretraining reaches average accuracy of 24.45% with linear probing and 49.62% after fine-tuning. That suggests the learned visual features carry useful interaction information, not merely details needed to reconstruct tactile patterns.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Does that establish an advantage over large visual-only pretraining?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: No. The comparison is among visual-tactile datasets, so it does not establish how TouchScale compares with large visual-only pretraining. The robot experiment is more direct about practical use. During mid-training, N-zero V-T-L-A predicts future tactile changes from current touch and visual-language context. Its main vision-language-action backbone stays frozen, and the human recordings provide no action labels. The model is then post-trained using robot demonstrations, alongside a baseline that skips this human-data stage.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The robot evaluation uses an x-arm six with a tactile-sensing hand, testing compliance sorting, bottle-cap removal, test-tube transfer, and whiteboard wiping. Each task has 50 teleoperated training demonstrations and 20 evaluation trials. Average success rises from 22.5% for the baseline to 57.5% after TouchScale mid-training. Success improves on every task, but the small task set and single robot platform mean these results should be treated as evidence of transfer in this setup, not a guarantee across robots.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Could the policy improve simply because tactile prediction gets better, or do we know that causes the success gains?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: We do not know that it causes them. The robot's future-tactile prediction improves after TouchScale mid-training, but after robot post-training its relationship with action-prediction error is weak. The data-scale experiment shows a broader upward pattern in task success, from 22.5% with no human mid-training to 57.5% with the full dataset, though some intermediate results level off. Better tactile prediction and better actions are associated here, but the mechanism remains uncertain.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: TouchScale connects naturally to work such as EgoDex and MAPLE, which use egocentric observations to learn manipulation-relevant representations. Its distinct emphasis is synchronized touch at scale, and its robot experiment avoids requiring human action retargeting. That makes it relevant where people can provide rich interaction recordings more readily than aligned human-and-robot demonstrations. The broader shift is from treating video as a complete record of interaction toward modeling what happens at contact, while still testing whether that information transfers to action.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: How far should we generalize from these results, given the limited robot tasks and the absence of human action labels?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Cautiously. Four tasks, 20 trials per task, and one robot embodiment cannot establish broad deployment performance. The dataset also does not include human action labels, so it cannot directly answer which human movements would help a robot most. Still, its consistent pipeline enables controlled data-scale comparisons, and its reconstructed object models may support further study. Independent tests across embodiments, settings, and tasks will be important for understanding where the gains persist.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The main takeaway is that touch can add supervision missing from ordinary first-person video, and that synchronized human touch may help a robot even when human actions are not labeled or mapped to robot commands. TouchScale provides a substantial resource and promising evidence across prediction, representation learning, and manipulation, while leaving important questions about generalization and causality open. The memorable point is simple: to understand physical interaction, seeing the hand move may not be enough; we may also need to measure what it feels.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Thanks for listening. If you have any further questions, ask our AI assistant or drop a comment.
